title: The Kindly Well
premise: Isandro Amberdale has spent twenty years as a hospice nurse listening to the dying count backwards from a number only they seem to know, and he has learned that when the count reaches zero, something arrives to collect. When his childhood imaginary friend, a tall figure called the Kindly Man, appears on his porch unchanged after three decades, Isandro is drawn back to Hollowmere, the village where six children vanished the winter he turned nine — and where he now realizes he was the one who invited the Kindly Well's keeper in. As the frost writes its patterns across windows and the last surviving villagers begin counting backwards in unison, Isandro must uncover what the adults of Hollowmere fed to the well to keep their own names off its ledger. In the end, Isandro chooses loyalty over survival: he gives the well his true name and memory of that winter, freeing the trapped children but erasing himself from every living recollection, so that the book closes on a village at sunrise where no one remembers why the doors are finally open.
about_author: Mara Vane is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent eleven years in palliative wards before turning to writing full-time. She lives on the coast of Maine, where she keeps an inventory of every door in her house and claims it is just a habit.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. On the night shift at Rosehaven Hospice, Isandro tends Mr. Ellery, who counts backwards from forty-one with increasing urgency. When the count hits zero, the cardiac monitor flatlines and every light in the wing dims for exactly nine seconds. Isandro logs it, locks the doors twice, and counts them. The beat is dread disguised as routine: we learn this has happened before, many times, and he has never told anyone.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Arriving home before dawn, Isandro finds a figure waiting on his porch — the Kindly Man, his childhood imaginary friend, identical down to the buttonless coat, though Isandro is thirty-eight. The figure says only, 'You left the door open in your heart, and I kept the appointment.' Isandro does not invite him in; he doesn't have to. The chapter ends with frost forming on the inside of the windows. Beat: uncanny homecoming.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: POV Isandro, with a fragmented childhood memory interleaved. Searching a locked box of his mother's effects, Isandro finds a photograph of Hollowmere's winter fair, 1994, six children circled in red ink — himself among them — and a page torn from a parish ledger reading 'the well takes what is freely given.' He remembers singing at the well as a child and nothing after. Beat: the horror shifts inward; he was a participant, not a witness.

chapters.title: Road to Hollowmere
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He drives to Hollowmere, finding it half-abandoned, streetlights burning at noon, doors painted over but never removed. At the village edge, a woman named Odile Crane recognizes him instantly and goes white: 'You're the ninth. You came back.' She refuses to explain, only warns him not to answer anyone who knocks after dark. Beat: dread of return; the past is not past here.

chapters.title: The Innkeeper's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Lodging at the Drowned Lamb inn, Isandro finds the old parish ledger hidden behind the bar, its pages recording 'gifts' given to the well each winter — livestock, heirlooms, and, starting in 1989, names. Six children's names follow six lean harvests. His own name is written in his mother's hand, dated the night before the disappearances stopped. Beat: betrayal; the parents bought safety with their children.

chapters.title: Odile's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Flashback chapter to winter 1994 through Odile's eyes as a young mother on the parish council: the drought of goodwill, the well-keeper's instructions delivered by a tall man in a buttonless coat, the vote to give names instead of goods. Odile wrote her own daughter's name and then, shamed, substituted a neighbor's child. Beat: guilt made flesh; the mechanics of the horror revealed without excusing it.

chapters.title: Six Empty Chairs
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Isandro interviews the surviving parents under hospice-nurse pretenses. Each begins, unprompted, counting backwards mid-conversation — different numbers, all approaching zero. One, Mrs. Aldous, breaks and tells him the children didn't die; they were 'kept,' because the well doesn't kill what it's given, it holds it. Beat: hope with teeth — rescue may be possible, which makes everything worse.

chapters.title: The Kindly Man Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The Kindly Man appears in his rented room, courteous, patient, answering questions only in riddles about debts and ledgers. He reveals Isandro wasn't taken because he was already 'half-given' — his mother gave his name but he refused to finish the gift by speaking it aloud at the well. The refusal is why the count never reached zero for him. Beat: Isandro learns his survival was an act of childish defiance he doesn't remember making.

chapters.title: Frost Patterns
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Frost begins writing legible patterns on every window in the village: columns of numbers, descending. The whole village can see them now. Odile confirms the countdown matches the ledger — when the frost reaches zero, the well 'closes its books' for another generation, taking everyone whose name remains outstanding. Isandro's name is still on the page. Beat: ticking clock made visible and communal.

chapters.title: The Well Itself
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Guided by Odile, Isandro reaches the well beyond the churchyard — dry, ringed in stones worn smooth like held hands. Listening at the mouth, he hears children's voices, unaged, singing the counting song. One voice calls his childhood nickname. He nearly answers. Odile drags him back: 'It wants you to say your name into it. That's how gifts are finished.' Beat: temptation; love weaponized.

chapters.title: Loyalty of the Damned
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile confesses fully to Isandro: her daughter Wren was one of the six, and Odile has spent thirty years leaving offerings, keeping the well 'warm' so Wren wouldn't be collected outright. She begs Isandro to let the countdown reach zero and take the outstanding names — including his — rather than disturb the arrangement. Her loyalty to her daughter versus the truth of what she did. Beat: antagonist with a sympathetic spine.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The village turns on Isandro, blaming him for the frost's acceleration — his return reactivated the debt. Someone nails his door shut from outside while he sleeps; the Kindly Man stands in the yard all night, unmoving, 'keeping the appointment.' Isandro realizes the villagers would rather feed him to the well than face the ledger themselves. Beat: isolation; justice outside the law begins to look like mob arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Ninth Name
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. In the parish records vault, Isandro finds the original gift-list and discovers a seventh name smudged out beneath the six — his mother's own. She tried to substitute herself, was refused (adults' names 'spoil'), and wrote his instead. The final entry in her handwriting: 'Forgive me. I could not finish it either.' Beat: grief reframed; his mother was a coward and a protector in the same stroke.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards Together
chapters.summary: POV ensemble, anchored on Isandro. That night, every remaining villager begins counting backwards aloud in their homes, synchronized, unable to stop — the well calling in its debts early because Isandro's presence 'reopened the account.' Odile's count starts lowest: eleven. Isandro sits with her, holding her hand, doing what he does best: staying with the dying. Beat: tenderness inside terror; his nurse's vocation becomes his moral center.

chapters.title: Wren at the Window
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile sees her daughter Wren at her window, still nine years old, mouthing 'Mama, it's cold.' Odile prepares to walk to the well and give herself in exchange, law or no law, ledger or no ledger. Isandro stops her with the truth she's avoided: the well doesn't trade, it only holds; her sacrifice would add a seventh prisoner, not free one. Beat: loyalty confronted with truth and forced to yield.

chapters.title: The Terms of Release
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The Kindly Man finally speaks plainly: the well releases what is given back if the giver completes the gift willingly — name, memory, and self, entire. Not death: erasure. The giver is unwritten from every mind and record. Isandro understands the price and hides it from Odile. He asks only one question: 'Will they remember being saved?' The Kindly Man: 'They will remember being cold, and then not cold.' Beat: quiet resolve; the sacrifice defined.

chapters.title: Zero Hour
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The frost reaches single digits. The village gathers at the churchyard in terrified silence, some praying, some holding ropes and stones — the old justice, ready to throw Isandro in whether he consents or not. Odile, seeing the rope, steps between him and the crowd and finally tells them all the truth of 1994, naming every parent who signed. Beat: truth spoken publicly at last; the mob falters.

chapters.title: Into the Kindly Well
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. At the well's mouth, Isandro speaks his full name — Isandro Amberdale, son of Maren, the ninth gift, the unfinished one — and offers it freely, then climbs down into the dry dark. The descent is dreamlike: corridors of frost, small hands taking his, six children singing the count upward now instead of down. Climax: the gift completed from inside, the reversal of the counting song.

chapters.title: Sunrise Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Dawn. The frost patterns vanish mid-stroke. The six children walk out of the churchyard mist, unaged, blinking — Wren first, running to Odile. The villagers embrace them and turn to thank Isandro and find no one there. His car is gone from the lane. His room at the inn is storeroom dust. Every photograph of him is blank paper. Beat: triumph braided with loss; the miracle and the cost in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Unremembered
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Weeks later, Hollowmere rebuilds. Odile alone retains a shape of grief without an object — she keeps setting a fourth cup at tea and cannot say why. She finds Isandro's hospice badge in the churchyard grass, reads the name, and the name slides off her memory like water. She buries the badge beneath the well's stones. Beat: mourning without a mourner's target; the theme of memory made intimate.

chapters.title: Rosehaven, Nights
chapters.summary: POV third-person limited on a new nurse, Priya, newly hired at Rosehaven Hospice. A dying patient counts backwards and reaches zero; the lights dim nine seconds. Priya mentions it to staff; no one named Isandro ever worked there, though his handwriting fills years of logbooks no one can attribute. On her first solo shift, Priya hears a knock at the station door after midnight and, remembering nothing else, counts the doors. Beat: the cycle persists; the reader knows what she doesn't.

chapters.title: The Open Door
chapters.summary: POV ambiguous, drifting between Priya and a presence. Final image: on a porch in Hollowmere at dusk, a door stands open that no one opened, and frost writes a single number on the glass — not a countdown, but a one, patient, unhurried. Somewhere, something kind and terrible waits for the next freely given invitation, and the last line notes that the well has always preferred volunteers. Beat: resolution with a held breath; horror restored to equilibrium.
